renders._yaml:
- component: advanced_viz
  id: coverage_heatmap
  title: Domain coverage per protein and database
  description: |-
    Each cell is the fraction of a protein's residues covered by the domains of one database, from 0 (no hit) to 1 (every residue covered), with the sample as a row strip. It answers which databases describe each protein and how completely.
    How to read: clustered, proteins that group together are described by the same databases. A protein bright in one column and blank in the others rests on a single source, and a blank row has no annotation at all, so open the domain architecture for it. A skipped database is a column of zeros.
    Lines and annotations: the dendrograms come from hierarchical clustering of the rows and columns. No cut-off is drawn, because no published rule defines a sufficient coverage.
  kind: complex_heatmap
  config:
    value_columns:
    - pfam
    - funfam
    - nmpfams
    - metagroot
    - interproscan
    row_annotation_cols:
    - sample
  roles:
    index: entity

- component: table
  title: Coverage table
  description: |-
    Each row is a protein with the fraction of its residues covered by each searched database. It answers the exact value behind a heatmap cell.
    How to read: sort a database column to find the best covered proteins, or sort ascending to list the poorly described ones.

- component: advanced_viz
  id: database_upset
  title: Database agreement
  description: |-
    Each bar is an intersection: the number of proteins annotated by exactly that set of databases, coloured by how many databases share them. It answers how far the databases agree on which proteins carry a domain.
    How to read: a tall bar with every dot joined is a well-known family that all databases describe. A tall single-dot bar is a protein only one database reaches, so its annotation rests on one source. Open the coverage heatmap to see how much of those proteins the single database covers.
    Lines and annotations: none are drawn. The side bars give the number of proteins each database annotates.
  kind: upset_plot
  config:
    set_columns:
    - pfam
    - funfam
    - nmpfams
    - metagroot
    - interproscan
    color_intersections_by: degree

- component: table
  title: Database membership table
  description: |-
    Each row is a protein with a 1 for every database that annotates at least one domain on it. It answers which databases cover a given protein.
    How to read: filter to a single database column to list the proteins only that source reaches.

- component: advanced_viz
  id: domain_record
  title: Domain record
  description: |-
    The card shows one domain span as labelled fields: its family, database, position, length, E-value and the part of the family model it matches. It answers what a single domain hit is.
    How to read: select a row in the table to fill it. A small fraction of the HMM covered means a partial match to the family, which deserves a second look in another database.
  kind: record_card
  config:
    labels:
      span: Span (residues)
      protein_length: Protein length (residues)
      evalue: E-value
      neg_log10_evalue: -log10 E-value
      hmm_coverage: Fraction of the HMM covered
      hmm_from: HMM start
      hmm_to: HMM end
      hmm_length: HMM length
  roles:
    id: domain_id
    title: label

- component: advanced_viz
  id: domain_significance
  title: Domain significance against length
  description: |-
    Each point is a domain span: its length in residues on the horizontal axis and the minus log10 of its independent E-value on the vertical axis, coloured by the database that reports it. It answers which domains are long and confident and which are weak.
    How to read: points high on the plot are strong matches. Long, high spans are whole-protein families and short, high ones are motifs. Weak points of any length are borderline, so check them in a second database.
    Lines and annotations: the horizontal line is an E-value of 0.01, the default inclusion threshold of HMMER (per-target and per-domain). HMMER applies it to the full-sequence and conditional E-values, so a few points can sit just below the line. InterProScan matches pass the filters of their own member database, not one shared E-value.
    Sources: http://eddylab.org/software/hmmer/Userguide.pdf and https://github.com/ebi-pf-team/interproscan-docs/blob/master/docs/FAQ.rst
  kind: scatter_xy
  config:
    x_title: Domain span (residues)
    y_title: -log10 E-value
    reference_line: horizontal
    reference_value: 2
    reference_label: E-value 0.01
    top_n_labels: 8
  roles:
    x: span
    y: neg_log10_evalue
    label: label
    color: database

- component: advanced_viz
  id: domain_architecture
  title: Domain architecture
  description: |-
    Each lane is a protein drawn to scale, with one block per domain coloured by family and placed at its start and end. It answers which domains a protein carries and in what order.
    How to read: proteins with the same block order share an architecture, so they probably share a function. A block drawn partly filled matches only part of its family model, and overlapping blocks from different databases describe the same region. Hover a block for its database, accession and E-value.
    Lines and annotations: a partly filled block shows the fraction of the family HMM that the match covers, from the hmmsearch alignment. No cut-off is drawn on this tile.
  kind: domain_architecture
  roles:
    entity: entity
    start: start
    end: end
    label: label
    protein_length: protein_length
    hmm_from: hmm_from
    hmm_to: hmm_to
    hmm_length: hmm_length
    hmm_coverage: hmm_coverage
    evalue: evalue
    source: source
    description: description
    accession: accession

- component: card
  id: domain_count
  title: Annotated proteins
  description: |-
    The hero number is the count of proteins with at least one domain, the second number counts every domain span, and the bars rank the databases by their domain spans. It answers how much annotation there is and which database provides most.
    How to read: a database with a long bar contributes most spans, which is not the same as the best coverage, so check the coverage heatmap.
  column: entity
  aggregation: nunique
  aggregations:
  - count
  secondary_layout: top_n
  breakdown_col: database
  top_n_count: 5
  caption: domains, by database

- component: card
  id: domain_families
  title: Distinct families
  description: |-
    The hero number is the count of distinct domain families, the second number counts every domain span, and the bars rank the sources by their spans. It answers how varied the annotation is and which library or member database reports most.
    How to read: many spans over few families means a few families repeat across the proteins.
  column: label
  aggregation: nunique
  aggregations:
  - count
  secondary_layout: top_n
  breakdown_col: source
  top_n_count: 5
  caption: domains, by source

- component: card
  id: domain_span
  title: Domain length
  description: |-
    The hero number is the median domain span in residues, and the box shows the spread. It answers how long a typical domain is.
    How to read: a short median with a long upper whisker means mostly motifs with a few whole-protein families. Open the significance plot to see which ones are confident.
  column: span
  aggregation: median
  aggregations:
  - box_plot_stats
  secondary_layout: box_plot
  caption: median, with its spread

- component: figure
  title: Domain length per database
  description: |-
    Each box is the spread of domain spans in residues for one database. It answers whether the databases describe domains of different sizes.
    How to read: a database with longer spans describes whole families, and one with short spans reports motifs or fragments. Compare boxes before combining counts across databases.
  visu_type: box
  dict_kwargs:
    x: database
    y: span
    color: database
    labels:
      database: Database
      span: Domain span (residues)

- component: table
  title: Domain table
  description: |-
    Each row is one domain span from one database, with its position, length, E-value and the part of the family model it matches. It answers the details behind every tile of this view, and a row selection fills the domain record.
    How to read: sort by E-value to list the strongest matches, or filter by database to compare sources.
  row_selection_enabled: true
  row_selection_column: domain_id

- component: advanced_viz
  id: protein_record
  title: Protein record
  description: |-
    The card shows one protein as labelled fields: its length, domain hits, how many databases annotate it, the share of its residues covered and the predicted secondary structure. It answers what is known about a single protein.
    How to read: select a row in the table or a point in the scatter to fill it. A protein with few databases and a low covered share is poorly described.
  kind: record_card
  config:
    labels:
      length: Length (residues)
      annotation_status: Annotation status
      domain_hits: Domain hits
      databases_hit: Databases with a hit
      annotated_residues: Residues covered by a domain
      annotated_pct: Residues covered by a domain (%)
      top_domain: Best domain
      top_domain_database: Best domain database
      top_domain_evalue: Best domain E-value
      helix_pct: Helix (%)
      strand_pct: Strand (%)
      coil_pct: Coil (%)
  roles:
    id: entity
    title: top_domain

- component: advanced_viz
  id: length_vs_cover
  title: Length against annotated share
  description: |-
    Each point is a protein: its length in residues against the percentage of its residues covered by at least one domain, coloured by the database of its best domain. It answers which proteins are well described and which carry long unannotated regions.
    How to read: short proteins at full coverage are single-domain proteins. Long proteins with low coverage carry regions no searched database describes, which makes them candidates for new domains or for a different database. Points without a best domain have no colour.
    Lines and annotations: none are drawn, because no published rule defines a sufficient coverage.
  kind: scatter_xy
  config:
    x_title: Protein length (residues)
    y_title: Residues covered by a domain (%)
    top_n_labels: 8
  roles:
    x: length
    y: annotated_pct
    label: entity
    color: top_domain_database

- component: card
  id: protein_count
  title: Domain hits
  description: |-
    The hero number is the total count of domain hits over the proteins, with the median per protein below it, and the bars rank the proteins by annotation status. It answers how much annotation there is and how many proteins have none.
    How to read: a long unannotated bar means many proteins no database describes. Open the scatter to see which ones are long.
  column: domain_hits
  aggregation: sum
  aggregations:
  - median
  secondary_layout: top_n
  breakdown_col: annotation_status
  top_n_count: 2
  caption: proteins, by annotation status

- component: card
  id: protein_length
  title: Protein length
  description: |-
    The hero number is the median protein length in residues, and the box shows the spread. It answers how long the proteins are.
    How to read: a very wide spread mixes short peptides with large multidomain proteins, which have different annotation rates.
  column: length
  aggregation: median
  aggregations:
  - box_plot_stats
  secondary_layout: box_plot
  caption: median, with its spread

- component: card
  id: annotated_cover
  title: Residues covered by a domain
  description: |-
    The hero number is the median percentage of a protein's residues covered by at least one domain, and the box shows the spread. It answers how completely the proteins are described.
    How to read: a high median means most of each protein is explained. A box reaching down to zero marks proteins with no annotation.
  column: annotated_pct
  aggregation: median
  aggregations:
  - box_plot_stats
  secondary_layout: box_plot
  caption: median, with its spread

- component: card
  id: databases_per_protein
  title: Databases per protein
  description: |-
    The hero number is the median count of databases with a hit on a protein, and the box shows the spread. It answers how many independent sources describe a typical protein.
    How to read: a higher count means the annotation is corroborated. A box at one means most proteins rest on a single source.
  column: databases_hit
  aggregation: median
  aggregations:
  - box_plot_stats
  secondary_layout: box_plot
  caption: median, with its spread

- component: card
  id: helix_share
  title: Helix content
  description: |-
    The hero number is the median percentage of residues S4PRED predicts as helix, and the box shows the spread. It answers how helical the proteins are.
    How to read: a wide spread mixes helical and non-helical proteins. Compare with the strand share to classify the fold.
  column: helix_pct
  aggregation: median
  aggregations:
  - box_plot_stats
  secondary_layout: box_plot
  caption: median, with its spread

- component: card
  id: strand_share
  title: Strand content
  description: |-
    The hero number is the median percentage of residues S4PRED predicts as strand, and the box shows the spread. It answers how much beta structure the proteins carry.
    How to read: a wide spread mixes beta-rich and beta-poor proteins. Compare with the helix share to classify the fold.
  column: strand_pct
  aggregation: median
  aggregations:
  - box_plot_stats
  secondary_layout: box_plot
  caption: median, with its spread

- component: figure
  title: Protein length distribution
  description: |-
    Each bar counts proteins in a length bin, split by annotation status. It answers whether unannotated proteins differ in length from the annotated ones.
    How to read: unannotated proteins piled at short lengths are often fragments or small peptides with no family. Unannotated proteins spread across all lengths point to missing database coverage.
  visu_type: histogram
  dict_kwargs:
    x: length
    color: annotation_status
    labels:
      length: Protein length (residues)
      annotation_status: Annotation status

- component: table
  title: Protein table
  description: |-
    Each row is a protein with its length, domain hits per database, annotated share, best domain and predicted secondary structure shares. It answers the exact values behind every tile of this view, and a row selection fills the protein record.
    How to read: sort by annotated share to find the poorly described proteins, or filter by status.
  row_selection_enabled: true
  row_selection_column: entity

- component: advanced_viz
  id: residue_sequence_track
  title: Sequence, structure and domains
  description: |-
    Each position is one residue of the shown protein, with the amino acid letter, the secondary structure state S4PRED predicts as a coloured lane and its probability as a line, plus a lane for the domains. It answers where the helices, strands and domains lie along the sequence.
    How to read: a high probability means a confident state, and a low one marks an uncertain stretch. Domains that coincide with helix or strand runs point to a folded region, and coil over a long unannotated stretch suggests a linker or a disordered region. Select a residue to follow it on the structure.
    Lines and annotations: none are drawn. The probability line is the S4PRED probability of the predicted state at each residue.
  kind: sequence_track
  config:
    value_label: S4PRED probability
  roles:
    position: position
    entity: entity
    residue: residue
    category: category
    value: value

- component: advanced_viz
  id: predicted_structure
  title: Predicted structure coloured by domain
  description: |-
    The protein is folded from its sequence and each residue is coloured by the best domain that covers it. It answers where in three dimensions the domains sit.
    How to read: domains that form compact blocks are folded units. Residues without a domain keep the neutral colour, so a large neutral region is a part no database describes. The structure is a prediction, so treat it as a guide and not as a measurement.
    Note: the structure is resolved by an external service, ESMFold on ESM Atlas, and stays off unless an administrator enables the resolver.
  kind: molecule_3d
  roles:
    position: position
    entity: entity
    category: domain
    sequence: sequence

- component: card
  id: residue_count
  title: Residues
  description: |-
    The hero number is the count of residues in view, the second number is the highest position and so the longest protein, and the bars rank the predicted secondary structure states by residue count. It answers how much sequence is covered and how it divides between helix, strand and coil.
    How to read: coil is usually the largest class. A balance shifted to helix or strand points to a structured protein.
  column: position
  aggregation: count
  aggregations:
  - max
  secondary_layout: top_n
  breakdown_col: category
  top_n_count: 3
  caption: residues, by predicted state

- component: figure
  title: Domain overlap per residue
  description: |-
    Each bar counts residues by the number of domains that overlap at them, split by predicted structure state. It answers how crowded the annotation is.
    How to read: most residues carry zero or one domain. A tail of residues under many domains marks regions several databases describe, or overlapping annotations of one family.
  visu_type: histogram
  dict_kwargs:
    x: domains_here
    color: category
    labels:
      domains_here: Overlapping domains at the residue
      category: Predicted state

- component: table
  title: Residue table
  description: |-
    Each row is one residue of a protein with its amino acid, predicted structure state and probability, best covering domain and the number of overlapping domains. It answers the exact annotation of any residue.
    How to read: filter to a protein, then sort by position to read it along the sequence.
  columns:
  - entity
  - sample
  - position
  - residue
  - category
  - value
  - domain
  - domain_database
  - domains_here

- component: card
  id: kept_proteins
  title: Proteins kept
  description: |-
    The hero number is the total count of sequences kept after the length and duplicate filter, with the median and largest per sample below it, and the histogram shows the samples. It answers how much sequence enters the annotation.
    How to read: a sample far below the others lost most of its sequences to the filter, so compare it with the removed count.
  column: kept_sequences
  aggregation: sum
  aggregations:
  - median
  - max
  secondary_layout: histogram
  caption: kept proteins per sample
  headline: true

- component: card
  id: kept_residues
  title: Residues kept
  description: |-
    The hero number is the total count of residues in the kept sequences, with the median and largest per sample below it, and the histogram shows the samples. It answers how large the annotated sequence set is.
    How to read: compare with the protein count to judge the mean length of what was kept.
  column: kept_residues
  aggregation: sum
  aggregations:
  - median
  - max
  secondary_layout: histogram
  caption: kept residues per sample

- component: card
  id: removed_sequences
  title: Sequences removed
  description: |-
    The hero number is the total count of sequences the length and duplicate filter removed, with the median and largest per sample below it, and the histogram shows the samples. It answers how much input was discarded.
    How to read: a sample with many removed sequences has many duplicates or sequences outside the length limits. Check the pipeline's minimum and maximum length settings.
  column: removed_sequences
  aggregation: sum
  aggregations:
  - median
  - max
  secondary_layout: histogram
  caption: removed sequences per sample

- component: card
  id: annotated_proteins
  title: Proteins annotated
  description: |-
    The hero number is the total count of proteins with at least one domain, with the median and largest per sample below it, and the histogram shows the samples. It answers how many proteins the databases describe.
    How to read: compare with the kept proteins to see the share left without annotation.
  column: annotated_proteins
  aggregation: sum
  aggregations:
  - median
  - max
  secondary_layout: histogram
  caption: annotated proteins per sample

- component: card
  id: annotated_share
  title: Share of proteins annotated
  description: |-
    The hero number is the median percentage of a sample's proteins that carry at least one domain, and the box shows the spread across samples. It answers how well the databases cover the sequences.
    How to read: a low value means many proteins fall outside the searched databases. Samples far below the others deserve a look at the input and at the databases that were skipped.
  column: annotated_protein_pct
  aggregation: median
  aggregations:
  - box_plot_stats
  secondary_layout: box_plot
  caption: median, with its spread
  headline: true

- component: card
  id: sample_mean_length
  title: Mean protein length
  description: |-
    The hero number is the median over the samples of their mean protein length in residues, and the box shows the spread. It answers how long the proteins are.
    How to read: a sample with a very different mean length may hold fragments or a different kind of sequence, which changes its annotation rate.
  column: mean_length
  aggregation: median
  aggregations:
  - box_plot_stats
  secondary_layout: box_plot
  caption: median, with its spread

- component: card
  id: sample_domain_hits
  title: Domain hits
  description: |-
    The hero number is the total count of domain hits over every database, with the median and largest per sample below it, and the histogram shows the samples. It answers how much annotation the run produced.
    How to read: one protein can carry many hits, so a high count does not mean a high annotated share.
  column: domain_hits
  aggregation: sum
  aggregations:
  - median
  - max
  secondary_layout: histogram
  caption: domain hits per sample

- component: figure
  title: Proteins kept per sample
  description: |-
    Each bar is a sample: the count of sequences kept after filtering, coloured by the percentage of its proteins that carry a domain. It answers which samples are large and how well each is annotated.
    How to read: a tall bar with a pale or dark colour at the low end of the scale is a large sample the databases describe poorly. No cut-off is drawn, because no published rule defines a sufficient annotated share.
    Lines and annotations: The dashed line is the median number of proteins kept of this table, a reference computed from the rows on show (it follows the filters), not a cut-off of the annotation pipeline.
  visu_type: bar
  dict_kwargs:
    x: sample_id
    y: kept_sequences
    color: annotated_protein_pct
    labels:
      sample_id: Sample
      kept_sequences: Proteins kept
      annotated_protein_pct: Proteins annotated (%)
  reference_lines:
  - axis: y
    stat: median
    column: kept_sequences

- component: table
  title: Sample table
  description: |-
    Each row is a sample with its sequences given and kept, residues, mean length and N50, and its annotated proteins and domain hits. It answers the exact values behind the tiles of this view.
    How to read: sort by annotated share to find the samples to inspect first.
  row_selection_enabled: true
  row_selection_column: sample_id

  caption: domains, by database

- component: card
  id: domain_families
  title: Distinct families
  description: |-
    The hero number is the count of distinct domain families, the second number counts every domain span, and the bars rank the sources by their spans. It answers how varied the annotation is and which library or member database reports most.
    How to read: many spans over few families means a few families repeat across the proteins.
  column: label
  aggregation: nunique
  aggregations:
  - count
  secondary_layout: top_n
  breakdown_col: source
  top_n_count: 5
  caption: domains, by source

- component: card
  id: domain_span
  title: Domain length
  description: |-
    The hero number is the median domain span in residues, and the box shows the spread. It answers how long a typical domain is.
    How to read: a short median with a long upper whisker means mostly motifs with a few whole-protein families. Open the significance plot to see which ones are confident.
  column: span
  aggregation: median
  aggregations:
  - box_plot_stats
  secondary_layout: box_plot
  caption: median, with its spread

- component: figure
  title: Domain length per database
  description: |-
    Each box is the spread of domain spans in residues for one database. It answers whether the databases describe domains of different sizes.
    How to read: a database with longer spans describes whole families, and one with short spans reports motifs or fragments. Compare boxes before combining counts across databases.
  visu_type: box
  dict_kwargs:
    x: database
    y: span
    color: database
    labels:
      database: Database
      span: Domain span (residues)

- component: table
  title: Domain table
  description: |-
    Each row is one domain span from one database, with its position, length, E-value and the part of the family model it matches. It answers the details behind every tile of this view, and a row selection fills the domain record.
    How to read: sort by E-value to list the strongest matches, or filter by database to compare sources.
  row_selection_enabled: true
  row_selection_column: domain_id

- component: advanced_viz
  id: protein_record
  title: Protein record
  description: |-
    The card shows one protein as labelled fields: its length, domain hits, how many databases annotate it, the share of its residues covered and the predicted secondary structure. It answers what is known about a single protein.
    How to read: select a row in the table or a point in the scatter to fill it. A protein with few databases and a low covered share is poorly described.
  kind: record_card
  config:
    labels:
      length: Length (residues)
      annotation_status: Annotation status
      domain_hits: Domain hits
      databases_hit: Databases with a hit
      annotated_residues: Residues covered by a domain
      annotated_pct: Residues covered by a domain (%)
      top_domain: Best domain
      top_domain_database: Best domain database
      top_domain_evalue: Best domain E-value
      helix_pct: Helix (%)
      strand_pct: Strand (%)
      coil_pct: Coil (%)
  roles:
    id: entity
    title: top_domain

- component: advanced_viz
  id: length_vs_cover
  title: Length against annotated share
  description: |-
    Each point is a protein: its length in residues against the percentage of its residues covered by at least one domain, coloured by the database of its best domain. It answers which proteins are well described and which carry long unannotated regions.
    How to read: short proteins at full coverage are single-domain proteins. Long proteins with low coverage carry regions no searched database describes, which makes them candidates for new domains or for a different database. Points without a best domain have no colour.
    Lines and annotations: none are drawn, because no published rule defines a sufficient coverage.
  kind: scatter_xy
  config:
    x_title: Protein length (residues)
    y_title: Residues covered by a domain (%)
    top_n_labels: 8
  roles:
    x: length
    y: annotated_pct
    label: entity
    color: top_domain_database

- component: card
  id: protein_count
  title: Domain hits
  description: |-
    The hero number is the total count of domain hits over the proteins, with the median per protein below it, and the bars rank the proteins by annotation status. It answers how much annotation there is and how many proteins have none.
    How to read: a long unannotated bar means many proteins no database describes. Open the scatter to see which ones are long.
  column: domain_hits
  aggregation: sum
  aggregations:
  - median
  secondary_layout: top_n
  breakdown_col: annotation_status
  top_n_count: 2
  caption: proteins, by annotation status

- component: card
  id: protein_length
  title: Protein length
  description: |-
    The hero number is the median protein length in residues, and the box shows the spread. It answers how long the proteins are.
    How to read: a very wide spread mixes short peptides with large multidomain proteins, which have different annotation rates.
  column: length
  aggregation: median
  aggregations:
  - box_plot_stats
  secondary_layout: box_plot
  caption: median, with its spread

- component: card
  id: annotated_cover
  title: Residues covered by a domain
  description: |-
    The hero number is the median percentage of a protein's residues covered by at least one domain, and the box shows the spread. It answers how completely the proteins are described.
    How to read: a high median means most of each protein is explained. A box reaching down to zero marks proteins with no annotation.
  column: annotated_pct
  aggregation: median
  aggregations:
  - box_plot_stats
  secondary_layout: box_plot
  caption: median, with its spread

- component: card
  id: databases_per_protein
  title: Databases per protein
  description: |-
    The hero number is the median count of databases with a hit on a protein, and the box shows the spread. It answers how many independent sources describe a typical protein.
    How to read: a higher count means the annotation is corroborated. A box at one means most proteins rest on a single source.
  column: databases_hit
  aggregation: median
  aggregations:
  - box_plot_stats
  secondary_layout: box_plot
  caption: median, with its spread

- component: card
  id: helix_share
  title: Helix content
  description: |-
    The hero number is the median percentage of residues S4PRED predicts as helix, and the box shows the spread. It answers how helical the proteins are.
    How to read: a wide spread mixes helical and non-helical proteins. Compare with the strand share to classify the fold.
  column: helix_pct
  aggregation: median
  aggregations:
  - box_plot_stats
  secondary_layout: box_plot
  caption: median, with its spread

- component: card
  id: strand_share
  title: Strand content
  description: |-
    The hero number is the median percentage of residues S4PRED predicts as strand, and the box shows the spread. It answers how much beta structure the proteins carry.
    How to read: a wide spread mixes beta-rich and beta-poor proteins. Compare with the helix share to classify the fold.
  column: strand_pct
  aggregation: median
  aggregations:
  - box_plot_stats
  secondary_layout: box_plot
  caption: median, with its spread

- component: figure
  title: Protein length distribution
  description: |-
    Each bar counts proteins in a length bin, split by annotation status. It answers whether unannotated proteins differ in length from the annotated ones.
    How to read: unannotated proteins piled at short lengths are often fragments or small peptides with no family. Unannotated proteins spread across all lengths point to missing database coverage.
  visu_type: histogram
  dict_kwargs:
    x: length
    color: annotation_status
    labels:
      length: Protein length (residues)
      annotation_status: Annotation status

- component: table
  title: Protein table
  description: |-
    Each row is a protein with its length, domain hits per database, annotated share, best domain and predicted secondary structure shares. It answers the exact values behind every tile of this view, and a row selection fills the protein record.
    How to read: sort by annotated share to find the poorly described proteins, or filter by status.
  row_selection_enabled: true
  row_selection_column: entity

- component: advanced_viz
  id: residue_sequence_track
  title: Sequence, structure and domains
  description: |-
    Each position is one residue of the shown protein, with the amino acid letter, the secondary structure state S4PRED predicts as a coloured lane and its probability as a line, plus a lane for the domains. It answers where the helices, strands and domains lie along the sequence.
    How to read: a high probability means a confident state, and a low one marks an uncertain stretch. Domains that coincide with helix or strand runs point to a folded region, and coil over a long unannotated stretch suggests a linker or a disordered region. Select a residue to follow it on the structure.
    Lines and annotations: none are drawn. The probability line is the S4PRED probability of the predicted state at each residue.
  kind: sequence_track
  config:
    value_label: S4PRED probability
  roles:
    position: position
    entity: entity
    residue: residue
    category: category
    value: value

- component: advanced_viz
  id: predicted_structure
  title: Predicted structure coloured by domain
  description: |-
    The protein is folded from its sequence and each residue is coloured by the best domain that covers it. It answers where in three dimensions the domains sit.
    How to read: domains that form compact blocks are folded units. Residues without a domain keep the neutral colour, so a large neutral region is a part no database describes. The structure is a prediction, so treat it as a guide and not as a measurement.
    Note: the structure is resolved by an external service, ESMFold on ESM Atlas, and stays off unless an administrator enables the resolver.
  kind: molecule_3d
  roles:
    position: position
    entity: entity
    category: domain
    sequence: sequence

- component: card
  id: residue_count
  title: Residues
  description: |-
    The hero number is the count of residues in view, the second number is the highest position and so the longest protein, and the bars rank the predicted secondary structure states by residue count. It answers how much sequence is covered and how it divides between helix, strand and coil.
    How to read: coil is usually the largest class. A balance shifted to helix or strand points to a structured protein.
  column: position
  aggregation: count
  aggregations:
  - max
  secondary_layout: top_n
  breakdown_col: category
  top_n_count: 3
  caption: residues, by predicted state

- component: figure
  title: Domain overlap per residue
  description: |-
    Each bar counts residues by the number of domains that overlap at them, split by predicted structure state. It answers how crowded the annotation is.
    How to read: most residues carry zero or one domain. A tail of residues under many domains marks regions several databases describe, or overlapping annotations of one family.
  visu_type: histogram
  dict_kwargs:
    x: domains_here
    color: category
    labels:
      domains_here: Overlapping domains at the residue
      category: Predicted state

- component: table
  title: Residue table
  description: |-
    Each row is one residue of a protein with its amino acid, predicted structure state and probability, best covering domain and the number of overlapping domains. It answers the exact annotation of any residue.
    How to read: filter to a protein, then sort by position to read it along the sequence.
  columns:
  - entity
  - sample
  - position
  - residue
  - category
  - value
  - domain
  - domain_database
  - domains_here

- component: card
  id: kept_proteins
  title: Proteins kept
  description: |-
    The hero number is the total count of sequences kept after the length and duplicate filter, with the median and largest per sample below it, and the histogram shows the samples. It answers how much sequence enters the annotation.
    How to read: a sample far below the others lost most of its sequences to the filter, so compare it with the removed count.
  column: kept_sequences
  aggregation: sum
  aggregations:
  - median
  - max
  secondary_layout: histogram
  caption: kept proteins per sample
  headline: true

- component: card
  id: kept_residues
  title: Residues kept
  description: |-
    The hero number is the total count of residues in the kept sequences, with the median and largest per sample below it, and the histogram shows the samples. It answers how large the annotated sequence set is.
    How to read: compare with the protein count to judge the mean length of what was kept.
  column: kept_residues
  aggregation: sum
  aggregations:
  - median
  - max
  secondary_layout: histogram
  caption: kept residues per sample

- component: card
  id: removed_sequences
  title: Sequences removed
  description: |-
    The hero number is the total count of sequences the length and duplicate filter removed, with the median and largest per sample below it, and the histogram shows the samples. It answers how much input was discarded.
    How to read: a sample with many removed sequences has many duplicates or sequences outside the length limits. Check the pipeline's minimum and maximum length settings.
  column: removed_sequences
  aggregation: sum
  aggregations:
  - median
  - max
  secondary_layout: histogram
  caption: removed sequences per sample

- component: card
  id: annotated_proteins
  title: Proteins annotated
  description: |-
    The hero number is the total count of proteins with at least one domain, with the median and largest per sample below it, and the histogram shows the samples. It answers how many proteins the databases describe.
    How to read: compare with the kept proteins to see the share left without annotation.
  column: annotated_proteins
  aggregation: sum
  aggregations:
  - median
  - max
  secondary_layout: histogram
  caption: annotated proteins per sample

- component: card
  id: annotated_share
  title: Share of proteins annotated
  description: |-
    The hero number is the median percentage of a sample's proteins that carry at least one domain, and the box shows the spread across samples. It answers how well the databases cover the sequences.
    How to read: a low value means many proteins fall outside the searched databases. Samples far below the others deserve a look at the input and at the databases that were skipped.
  column: annotated_protein_pct
  aggregation: median
  aggregations:
  - box_plot_stats
  secondary_layout: box_plot
  caption: median, with its spread
  headline: true

- component: card
  id: sample_mean_length
  title: Mean protein length
  description: |-
    The hero number is the median over the samples of their mean protein length in residues, and the box shows the spread. It answers how long the proteins are.
    How to read: a sample with a very different mean length may hold fragments or a different kind of sequence, which changes its annotation rate.
  column: mean_length
  aggregation: median
  aggregations:
  - box_plot_stats
  secondary_layout: box_plot
  caption: median, with its spread

- component: card
  id: sample_domain_hits
  title: Domain hits
  description: |-
    The hero number is the total count of domain hits over every database, with the median and largest per sample below it, and the histogram shows the samples. It answers how much annotation the run produced.
    How to read: one protein can carry many hits, so a high count does not mean a high annotated share.
  column: domain_hits
  aggregation: sum
  aggregations:
  - median
  - max
  secondary_layout: histogram
  caption: domain hits per sample

- component: figure
  title: Proteins kept per sample
  description: |-
    Each bar is a sample: the count of sequences kept after filtering, coloured by the percentage of its proteins that carry a domain. It answers which samples are large and how well each is annotated.
    How to read: a tall bar with a pale or dark colour at the low end of the scale is a large sample the databases describe poorly. No cut-off is drawn, because no published rule defines a sufficient annotated share.
    Lines and annotations: The dashed line is the median number of proteins kept of this table, a reference computed from the rows on show (it follows the filters), not a cut-off of the annotation pipeline.
  visu_type: bar
  dict_kwargs:
    x: sample_id
    y: kept_sequences
    color: annotated_protein_pct
    labels:
      sample_id: Sample
      kept_sequences: Proteins kept
      annotated_protein_pct: Proteins annotated (%)
  reference_lines:
  - axis: y
    stat: median
    column: kept_sequences

- component: table
  title: Sample table
  description: |-
    Each row is a sample with its sequences given and kept, residues, mean length and N50, and its annotated proteins and domain hits. It answers the exact values behind the tiles of this view.
    How to read: sort by annotated share to find the samples to inspect first.
  row_selection_enabled: true
  row_selection_column: sample_id
